claim: Sir2 is required for both transcriptional silencing and late replication at the repetitive ribosomal DNA (rDNA) arrays in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the histone deacetylase Sir2 is required for both transcriptional silencing and late replication at the repetitive ribosomal DNA (rDNA) arrays.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about Sir2's function.

claim: In the absence of SIR2, a de-repressed RNA PolII repositions MCM replicative helicases from their loading site at the ribosomal origin to an adjacent region with lower nucleosome occupancy.
source: We have previously reported that in the absence of SIR2, a de-repressed RNA PolII repositions MCM replicative helicases from their loading site at the ribosomal origin, where they abut well-positioned, high-occupancy nucleosomes, to an adjacent region with lower nucleosome occupancy.
evidence: This is stated as a previously reported finding by the authors, supported by citation to their prior work.

claim: The displaced MCMs at rDNA origins have increased firing propensity compared to the nondisplaced MCMs.
source: here we show that the displaced MCMs at rDNA origins have increased firing propensity compared to the nondisplaced MCMs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both activation of the repositioned MCMs and low occupancy of the adjacent nucleosomes critically depend on the chromatin remodeling activity of FUN30.
source: Furthermore, we found that both activation of the repositioned MCMs and low occupancy of the adjacent nucleosomes critically depend on the chromatin remodeling activity of FUN30.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing effects of FUN30 deletion.

claim: Sir2 delays replication timing through a mechanism involving MCM helicase positioning and nucleosome occupancy.
source: Our study elucidates the mechanism by which Sir2 delays replication timing
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental findings presented.

claim: Activation of a specific replication origin in vivo relies on the nucleosome context shaped by a single chromatin remodeler.
source: it demonstrates, for the first time, that activation of a specific replication origin in vivo relies on the nucleosome context shaped by a single chromatin remodeler.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study, supported by the Fun30 experiments.

claim: SIR2 was initially identified in budding yeast in 1979 on the basis of its role in transcriptional repression at the silent mating type loci.
source: SIR2 was initially identified in budding yeast in 1979 on the basis of its role in transcriptional repression at the silent mating type loci (Haber and George, 1979; Klar et al., 1979; Rine et al., 1979)
evidence: This is a historical fact supported by citations to the original discovery papers.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 not only activates transcription at the silent mating type loci but also abolishes their heterochromatic structure.
source: deletion of SIR2 not only activates their transcription but also abolishes their heterochromatic structure (Ivy et al., 1986; Rine and Herskowitz, 1987; Weiss and Simpson, 1998; Ravindra et al., 1999; Haber, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Sir2 regulates DNA replication at the silent mating type loci, telomeres, and the rDNA.
source: It was later discovered that, in addition to regulating transcription at the silent mating type loci, Sir2 also regulates DNA replication, and it does so not only at the silent mating type loci but also at the two other heterochromatic regions of the yeast genome, namely at telomeres and the rDNA (Pasero et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The rDNA is composed of approximately 150 tandemly arranged 9.1 kb repeats.
source: The rDNA, which encodes the structural RNA components of the ribosome, is composed of approximately 150 tandemly arranged 9.1 kb repeats (Woolford and Baserga, 2013).
evidence: This is a known structural feature of the rDNA, supported by citation.

claim: The rDNA is almost 1.4 megabases in size.
source: At almost 1.4 megabases, the rDNA is too large to be replicated passively, and thus it must contain its own origins of replication.
evidence: This is calculated from the number of repeats and their size, representing established knowledge.

claim: The ribosomal RNAs are produced as two major species, known as the 35S and 5S, which are transcribed by RNA PolI and RNA PolIII, respectively.
source: The ribosomal RNAs are produced as two major species, known as the 35S and 5S, which are transcribed by RNA PolI and RNA PolIII, respectively (Fernández-Pevida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rRNA transcription, supported by citation.

claim: Between the 5' ends of the 35S and 5S genes is an origin of replication.
source: Between the 5' ends of these genes is an origin of replication
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: Immediately to the left of the rDNA origin is a short Sir2-repressed RNA PolII-transcribed noncoding transcript called C-pro.
source: immediately to the left of this origin is a short Sir2-repressed RNA PolII-transcribed noncoding transcript called C-pro (Kobayashi and Ganley, 2005; Li et al., 2006; Vasiljeva et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies that characterized C-pro.

claim: In wild-type cells, rDNA origins fire in the second half of S phase, making the rDNA among the later replicating regions of the genome.
source: In wild-type (WT) cells, rDNA origins fire in the second half of S phase, making the rDNA among the later replicating regions of the genome, while in sir2 mutants, they fire early in S phase (Pasero et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2014; Foss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: In sir2 mutants, rDNA origins fire early in S phase.
source: In wild-type (WT) cells, rDNA origins fire in the second half of S phase, making the rDNA among the later replicating regions of the genome, while in sir2 mutants, they fire early in S phase (Pasero et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2014; Foss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: A point mutation at the rARS that decreased origin activity at the rDNA increased origin activity elsewhere in the genome and prolonged replicative lifespan.
source: By measuring lifespan in segregants from a cross between two genetically diverse strains of yeast, Kwan et al. were able to identify a point mutation at the rARS that (1) decreased origin activity at the rDNA; (2) increased origin activity elsewhere in the genome; and (3) prolonged replicative lifespan.
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Kwan et al., 2013.

claim: The 150 origins at the rDNA make up approximately one-third of total origins in yeast.
source: Most replication outside of the rDNA initiates from approximately 300 replication origins, and thus the 150 origins at the rDNA make up approximately one-third of total origins.
evidence: This is a calculation based on known numbers of origins in the yeast genome.

claim: Origin licensing refers to loading of the replicative helicase in G1.
source: Origin licensing refers to loading of the replicative helicase in G1, and only origins that have been licensed are capable of being used in the subsequent S phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA replication.

claim: Only origins that have been licensed are capable of being used in the subsequent S phase.
source: Origin licensing refers to loading of the replicative helicase in G1, and only origins that have been licensed are capable of being used in the subsequent S phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA replication.

claim: Licensing occurs when an origin recognition complex, Orc1-6, that is bound to an ARS consensus sequence within the origin loads two hexameric helicases, each consisting of a ring of subunits, MCM2-7, that encircles the DNA.
source: Licensing occurs when an origin recognition complex, Orc1-6, that is bound to an 11–17 base pair so-called ARS consensus sequence (ACS) within the origin loads two hexameric helicases, each consisting of a ring of subunits, MCM2-7, that encircles the DNA (Bell and Stillman, 1992; Francis et al., 2009; Bell and Botchan, 2013; Deegan and Diffley, 2016; Deegan et al., 2016; Douglas et al., 2018; Lewis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of origin licensing, supported by multiple citations.

claim: DNA replication initiates from only a subset of licensed origins, namely those where the helicase complex is activated, a process referred to as origin firing.
source: DNA replication initiates from only a subset of these licensed origins, namely those where the helicase complex is activated, a process referred to as origin firing (Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about DNA replication, supported by citation.

claim: Origin firing is triggered by activation of two kinase signaling pathways, DDK and CDK.
source: Origin firing is triggered by activation of two kinase signaling pathways, DDK and CDK, which then cause each hexameric MCM helicase to encircle a single strand of DNA and track in opposite directions in front of the replisome, thereby establishing bidirectional replication (Heller et al., 2011; Duncker, 2016; Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about origin firing, supported by citations.

claim: Firing factors are not present in sufficient quantities to activate all licensed origins simultaneously.
source: Firing factors are not present in sufficient quantities to activate all licensed origins simultaneously, and thus origins are activated in waves, with firing factors being recycled until the entire genome has been replicated (Mantiero et al., 2011; Tanaka et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about origin firing, supported by citations.

claim: If the competition between the origins at the rDNA and those in the rest of the genome is tilted in favor of the rDNA, replication gaps between distantly spaced origins outside of the rDNA persist late into S phase.
source: Importantly, if the competition between the origins at the rDNA and those in the rest of the genome is tilted in favor of the rDNA, either by a point mutation in the rARS or by deletion of SIR2, replication gaps between distantly spaced origins outside of the rDNA persist late into S phase, and genome duplication may remain incomplete when the cell enters mitosis (Foss et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Weakening the rARS by a point mutation can suppress the short replicative lifespan characteristic of sir2 mutants.
source: Indeed, the observation that weakening the rARS by a point mutation can suppress the short replicative lifespan characteristic of sir2 mutants suggests that these replication gaps may be the ultimate cause of 'replicative death'.
evidence: This is based on observations from prior studies and leads to an inference about the cause of replicative death.

claim: Heterochromatic regions are late replicating in mammalian cells.
source: Consistent with this view of the utility of assigning a low priority to replication of repetitive sequence, heterochromatic regions are also late replicating in mammalian cells, and disease states have been associated with disruption of this pattern (Donley and Thayer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Disease states have been associated with disruption of late replication of heterochromatic regions in mammalian cells.
source: Consistent with this view of the utility of assigning a low priority to replication of repetitive sequence, heterochromatic regions are also late replicating in mammalian cells, and disease states have been associated with disruption of this pattern (Donley and Thayer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 abolishes heterochromatic compaction.
source: Consistent with this model, deletion of SIR2 abolishes heterochromatic compaction and simultaneously increases the ability of methylases and restriction endonucleases to act on those sequences (Gottschling, 1992; Singh and Klar, 1992; Loo and Rine, 1994; Weiss and Simpson, 1998; Ansari and Gartenberg, 1999; Ravindra et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Sir3 and Sir4 are not present at the rDNA.
source: In contrast, Sir3 and Sir4 are not present at the rDNA (Straight et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: rDNA is the most highly transcribed region of the genome, with transcription by PolI and PolIII accounting for approximately 80% of cellular RNA.
source: Moreover, rDNA is the most highly transcribed region of the genome, with transcription by PolI and PolIII accounting for approximately 80% of cellular RNA (Warner, 1999; Woolford and Baserga, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about rDNA transcription, supported by citations.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 increases accessibility of restriction enzymes to heterochromatin at the HML locus by 1.5-fold.
source: Additionally, deletion of SIR2 increases accessibility of restriction enzymes to heterochromatin at the HML locus by 1.5-fold, yet it increases PolII transcription by over 3000-fold (Holland, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 increases PolII transcription at the HML locus by over 3000-fold.
source: Additionally, deletion of SIR2 increases accessibility of restriction enzymes to heterochromatin at the HML locus by 1.5-fold, yet it increases PolII transcription by over 3000-fold (Holland, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: In WT cells, the MCM helicase complexes are located almost exclusively immediately adjacent to a high-occupancy well-positioned nucleosome approximately 130 base pairs to the left of the ACS.
source: This analysis revealed that, while deletion of SIR2 did not elicit an obvious change in the overall levels of licensing at the rDNA, it led to a dramatic redistribution of MCM helicase complexes: In WT cells, the helicase complexes are located almost exclusively immediately adjacent to a high-occupancy well-positioned nucleosome approximately 130 base pairs to the left of the ACS.
evidence: This is based on data from a prior study by the authors.

claim: In sir2 mutants, the MCM complexes are largely displaced to the right into an area with lower nucleosome occupancy.
source: In contrast, the MCM complexes in sir2 mutants are largely displaced to the right into an area with lower nucleosome occupancy (see Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on data from a prior study by the authors and shown in figures.

claim: The displacement of MCM complexes in sir2 mutants appears to be caused by the de-repression of C-pro transcription.
source: This displacement appears to be caused by the de-repression of C-pro transcription in the absence of SIR2, which results in RNA PolII pushing the MCM double-hexamer into the relatively nucleosome-free region.
evidence: This is based on inference from data in a prior study by the authors.

claim: The arrangement of MCM-proximal nucleosomes can have a dramatic effect on MCM activation.
source: This observation is provocative in light of studies demonstrating that the arrangement of MCM-proximal nucleosomes can have a dramatic effect on MCM activation (Azmi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Activation of an MCM double-hexamer loaded at an origin could be inhibited by nucleosomes arranged by specific chromatin remodeling enzymes.
source: Specifically, by using chromatin remodeling enzymes (CREs) to create a variety of nucleosomal arrangements on an origin-containing fragment of DNA, Azmi et al. demonstrated that activation of an MCM double-hexamer loaded at that origin could be inhibited by nucleosomes arranged by specific CREs.
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Azmi et al., 2017.

claim: A mutant version of Orc1 that alters phasing of MCM adjacent nucleosomes inhibits DNA replication in vivo and in vitro.
source: In another study (Chacin et al., 2023), a mutant version of Orc1 that retains the ability to load MCM but alters phasing of MCM adjacent nucleosomes was shown to inhibit DNA replication in vivo and in vitro, consistent with a critical role for nucleosome organization at origins in the initiation of replication.
evidence: This is based on a cited study by Chacin et al., 2023.

claim: Deletion of FUN30, but no other chromatin remodeling enzyme gene tested, delayed replication of the rDNA in a sir2 background.
source: To identify potential chromatin remodelers required for early rDNA replication in sir2, we measured rDNA replication timing in double mutants in sir2 and each of nine nonessential CRE subunits (Chd1, Fun30, Htl1, Irc5, Isw1, Isw2, Nhp10, Swr1, and Swp82). Deletion of FUN30, but no other gene, delayed replication of the rDNA in a sir2 background, shifting the Trel value from 1.2 to 1.06, while having had no significant effect in SIR2 cells (0.89 for WT and 0.91 for fun30) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A point mutation that abolishes Fun30 ATPase activity (K603R) suppresses early rDNA replication in sir2 mutants.
source: However, we found that a point mutation that abolishes Fun30 ATPase activity, K603R (Neves-Costa et al., 2009; Eapen et al., 2012), also suppresses early rDNA replication (Figure 2B), arguing that Fun30 instead promotes rDNA replication through its enzymatic activity in nucleosome remodeling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-phosphorylatable mutations in Fun30 (S20A and S28A) had no effect on the rDNA replication phenotype in sir2 mutants.
source: To determine whether the replication phenotype that we observed might be a consequence of Fun30's role in the DNA damage response, we tested non-phosphorylatable mutants for the ability to suppress early replication of the rDNA in sir2; these mutations had no effect on the replication phenotype (Figure 2B), arguing against a primary role for Fun30 in DNA damage repair that somehow manifests itself in replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 had no notable effect on rDNA size in a SIR2 strain.
source: While deletion of FUN30 had no notable effect on rDNA size in a SIR2 strain, it caused a 50% reduction in a sir2 mutant, from 9.2% to 4.2% (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 caused a 50% reduction in rDNA size in a sir2 mutant.
source: While deletion of FUN30 had no notable effect on rDNA size in a SIR2 strain, it caused a 50% reduction in a sir2 mutant, from 9.2% to 4.2% (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The rDNA size in fun30 sir2 mutants is estimated to be approximately 40 repeats.
source: Based on measurements in log-growing cells, we estimated the rDNA size in fun30 sir2 mutants to be ~40 repeats (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in the supplementary figure.

claim: Deletion of FOB1 does not prevent rDNA shrinkage in sir2 fun30 mutants, although it retards the transition to reduced array sizes.
source: To determine whether the reduction of rDNA size in sir2 fun30 mutants was dependent on RFB activity and FOB1, we deleted FUN30 in a sir2 fob1 strain with 160 repeats. Using this strategy, we obtained fob1 sir2 fun30 transformants with over 150 rDNA repeats. If rDNA shrinkage does not require Fob1, it should occur, albeit slowly, in fob1 mutants. To assess this, we continuously grew several independent fob1 sir2 fun30 colonies, along with control fob1 sir2, and fob1 fun30 strains for 120 generations. We found that, unlike the control fob1 strains, which maintained a stable rDNA size, all four fob1 sir2 fun30 cultures reduced their rDNA arrays size to fewer than 100 copies by 120 division (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Licensing at the rDNA is high, at approximately 60-85%, in WT, sir2, fun30, and sir2 fun30 cells.
source: Activation of MNase in all four genotypes led to an ~60–85% decrease in the XmnI fragment (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), therefore we conclude that (1) licensing is high, at ~60–85%; and (2) a much higher fraction of origins are licensed than are activated, making it unlikely that significant regulation of origin activity occurs at the level of licensing.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A much higher fraction of rDNA origins are licensed than are activated.
source: Activation of MNase in all four genotypes led to an ~60–85% decrease in the XmnI fragment (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), therefore we conclude that (1) licensing is high, at ~60–85%; and (2) a much higher fraction of origins are licensed than are activated, making it unlikely that significant regulation of origin activity occurs at the level of licensing.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing high licensing but known low activation.

claim: Deletion of SIR2 increased the number of activated rDNA origins 6.3-fold compared to WT.
source: When analyzed in aggregate at 20, 30, 60, and 90 min following release into HU, the average number of activated rDNA origins in sir2 mutant was increased 6.3-fold compared to those in WT (5.0±2.3 in sir2 vs 0.8±0.4 in WT, p<0.05 by two-tailed t-test)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from 2D gels.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 reduced the increased number of activated rDNA origins in sir2 mutants.
source: and this increased number was reduced upon FUN30 deletion (1.3±0.7 in sir2 fun30, p<0.05 by two-tailed t-test vs sir2, NS for comparison to WT).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from 2D gels.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 in a sir2 background partially restored EdU incorporation at early origins.
source: Deletion of FUN30 in a sir2 background partially restored EdU incorporation at early origins, concomitant with reduced EdU incorporation at rDNA origins.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from EdU-seq.

claim: The disappearance of the MCM-ChEC signal as cells progress through S phase can be used to assess origin firing.
source: We conclude that the disappearance of the MCM-ChEC signal as cells progress through S phase can be used to assess origin firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental validation showing that MCM signal decreases more at early origins than late origins.

claim: The displaced MCM2-ChEC signal in sir2 disappears more rapidly than its nondisplaced counterpart.
source: The MCM-ChEC signal in WT cells remained at their initial loading throughout the duration of the HU experiment (blue box in Figure 5C) as we have seen by ChIP in WT cells at 60 min. (Note that 200 mM HU causes an approximately 20-fold slowing of S phase, therefore a 60 min time point is equivalent to <5 min without HU, i.e. prior to the time when the rDNA origin fires in WT cells.) Like in WT, this nondisplaced population of MCM in sir2 remains relatively constant (blue box); however, in striking contrast, the displaced population of MCM in sir2 (orange box) shows a continual decrease over the course of the experiment
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 suppresses the early disappearance of the displaced MCM signal in sir2 mutants.
source: Furthermore, both the decrease in the displaced signal (orange box) and its corresponding increase upstream of the RFB were suppressed by deletion of FUN30.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The displaced population of MCM in sir2 cells fires more readily than its nondisplaced counterpart.
source: Taken together, these observations provide strong support for the hypothesis that the displaced population of MCM in sir2 cells fires more readily than its nondisplaced counterpart and that the increased firing of the displaced MCMs is suppressed by FUN30 deletion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing differential disappearance of MCM signals.

claim: In WT cells, a small fraction of MCM complexes are displaced, and this minor signal disappears more rapidly than its nondisplaced counterpart.
source: It is notable that, although a small fraction of the total G1 signal in WT arises from the displaced location, this minor signal likewise disappears more rapidly than its nondisplaced counterpart (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: C-pro RNA levels were approximately twice as high in sir2 fun30 cells compared to sir2 cells when adjusted for rDNA size.
source: Consistent with previous reports that fun30 mutants are deficient in transcriptional silencing (Neves-Costa et al., 2009), C-pro RNA levels were approximately twice as high in sir2 fun30 cells compared to sir2 cells when adjusted for rDNA size (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Deletion of FUN30 shifts the MCM distribution toward the repositioned MCM location over the non-repositioned one in G1 cells.
source: Moreover, deletion of FUN30 shifts the distribution toward the repositioned MCM location over the non-repositioned one in G1 cells (Figure 5C), aligning with the increased C-pro transcription observed in fun30 mutants.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Nucleosome occupancy at the +2 and +3 positions is higher in the sir2 fun30 double mutant than in the sir2 single mutant.
source: Plotting nucleosome midpoints at the rARS in G1 cells (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) reveals that nucleosome occupancy at the +2 (green box) and +3 (red box) positions is higher in the sir2 fun30 double mutant than in the sir2 single mutant.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Nucleosome occupancy is modestly increased in fun30 cells compared to WT cells.
source: Furthermore, this effect of Fun30 is not limited to the sir2 background, since nucleosome occupancy is also modestly increased in fun30 cells compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from MNase-seq.

claim: Fun30 is required for maintaining the low nucleosome occupancy in the region into which the preponderance of MCM complexes have been displaced in sir2 mutant cells.
source: This finding indicates that Fun30 is required for maintaining the low nucleosome occupancy in the region into which the preponderance of MCM complexes have been displaced in sir2 mutant cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing increased nucleosome occupancy in sir2 fun30 mutants.

claim: Only approximately 20% of potential rDNA origins are activated during any single S phase in WT cells.
source: It has been estimated that ~20% of potential rDNA origins are activated during any single S phase in WT cells (Brewer and Fangman, 1988; Linskens and Huberman, 1988).
evidence: This is based on cited studies using EM and 2D gel electrophoresis.

claim: The fraction of active rDNA origins is increased in sir2 mutant cells.
source: Furthermore, single-molecule studies suggested that the fraction of active origins is increased in sir2 mutant cells (Pasero et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited single-molecule studies.

claim: Regulation of rDNA replication initiation occurs primarily at the level of origin firing rather than licensing.
source: Our measurements of rDNA licensing showed that MCM are loaded in up to 90% of origins in WT cells and allowed us to conclude that regulation or rDNA replication initiation occurs primarily at the level of origin firing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing high licensing but low activation.

claim: The effect of Fun30 on DNA replication is remarkably specific to nucleosomes adjacent to repositioned MCM complexes at the rDNA.
source: In contrast, the effect of a chromatin remodeler on DNA replication we describe in this work is remarkably specific: we found that the activity of a single remodeler, Fun30, is required to activation not only of a specific origin, but that its action is specific to nucleosomes adjacent to repositioned MCM complexes at the rDNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: The suppression of rDNA origin activity in sir2 mutants by FUN30 deletion is so severe that it reduces the rDNA size approximately 3- to 5-fold.
source: The suppression of rDNA origin activity in sir2 mutants, which contained a large fraction of repositioned MCMs, by FUN30 deletion is so severe that it reduces the rDNA size ~3- to 5-fold, from 160 to 35–50 copies.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements of rDNA size.

claim: Even in WT cells, it is predominantly from MCMs that are displaced, likely due to low level of C-pro transcription, that replication initiates.
source: This has the important implication that the manner in which the rDNA origin fires in sir2 mutants may be simply an exaggerated instance of its normal behavior, and that even in WT cells, it is predominantly from MCMs that are displaced, likely due to low level of C-pro transcription, that replication initiates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that displaced MCMs fire earlier even in WT cells.

claim: This is the first in vivo demonstration of the modulation of an origin activity by a specific chromatin remodeler.
source: This is the first in vivo demonstration of the modulation of an origin activity by a specific chromatin remodeler in vivo, and has implications for the broader relationship between transcription and replication timing.
evidence: This is stated as a novel contribution of the study.
